title: Duchy of Brunswick
capsule: The Duchy of Brunswick was a German principality established by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 as successor to the Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, ruled by the House of Welf with its capital at Braunschweig. Duke Charles II was driven from his palace and forced to flee in 1830 following popular unrest, and was succeeded by his more conciliatory brother William VIII, whose reign of over fifty years brought relative stability. A protracted succession dispute between 1884 and 1913—arising from Prussian exclusion of the Hanoverian Welf claimants—left the duchy under consecutive regencies before Ernest Augustus finally acceded in 1913. He abdicated on 8 November 1918 during the German Revolution, and Brunswick became a free state within the Weimar Republic before merging into Lower Saxony in 1946.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The duchy's territory is well defined through Congress of Vienna instruments and subsequent German Confederation documentation; boundaries are among the most precisely attested of the German states in the nineteenth century.
